title: The Impossible Route: the Roaring Forties, Three Capes, and One Man Without a Radio
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Buenos Aires, born in Palermo
stops.date_confidence: attested; pinned to the atlas's canonical Buenos Aires anchor rather than to Palermo's own -34.5875 / -58.4205
stops.campa: In the Palermo barrio of Buenos Aires, to Victorio Dumas and Vicenta Grillo, a son is born into a family that has already lost its money. The atlas pins him where it pins Jorge Luis Borges born in 1899, Victoria Ocampo born in 1890, Bernardo Houssay, and San Martin coming ashore in 1812: one inherited coordinate on the Buenos Aires waterfront, standing in for a city. The boy will teach himself to box, to swim, to run and to fly. He will study at the Academia de Bellas Artes. He will not touch the open sea until he is thirty-one years old.
suggested_refs: Birth register of the Palermo parish, Buenos Aires, 26 September 1900

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the floors and the brass
stops.date_confidence: undated in source; placed in his boyhood after the family's ruin, defaulted to January
stops.campa: The fortune is gone before he is old enough to have spent any of it. He cleans floors, runs errands, and polishes the brass plates of shopfronts. Nothing in the record says when he first steps into a boat, and nothing names anyone who taught him to do anything. What the record does keep is the pattern of the years after this one: he takes up boxing, swimming, athletics and aviation, and he takes each of them up alone, without instruction, and without announcing beforehand what he means to do with it.
stops.quote: Tuve que limpiar pisos, hacer mandados, lustrar chapas de bronce de algun negocio.
stops.quote_source: Vito Dumas on his youth, quoted in es.wikipedia.org, 'Vito Dumas', footnote 3
suggested_refs: Revista Todo es Historia, no. 10, February 1968, the interview material behind the Dumas quotations

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the championship his widow remembers
stops.date_confidence: reported only by his widow, decades later; no competition, sanctioning body, distance or time is named anywhere reachable
stops.campa: His widow, eight years younger than he was, tells the story afterward: that in 1925 he was world champion of endurance in the water. No competition is named, no distance, no time, no body that sanctioned it. The claim rests on one person remembering. She remembers other things with more edge. He painted and sculpted, he built a radio set without having studied radio, and whatever he set himself to do he did. What he lacked, she says, was constancy and discipline, beginning everything in euphoria and abandoning it without warning.
stops.quote: Era un hombre muy activo. Le gustaban los deportes. Ademas pintaba, hacia escultura. Curso estudios en la Academia de Bellas Artes. Lo que se proponia lo hacia. Una vez, sin haber estudiado nunca nada sobre radio, armo un aparato. Lo que le faltaba era constancia, disciplina.
stops.quote_source: Dumas's widow, quoted in es.wikipedia.org, 'Vito Dumas', footnote 2
suggested_refs: Any Argentine swimming federation record for 1925 that would confirm or dissolve the endurance title

segments.name: The Lehg, Arcachon to the Plate

stops.name: Arcachon, the eight-metre sloop sails
stops.date_confidence: attested in both the Spanish and English accounts
stops.campa: He has never sailed the open sea. In the basin at Arcachon lies a French-built sloop of 1918, an International Eight Metre of some fifteen metres overall and two and a bit in the beam. He names her Lehg and takes her out alone into the Bay of Biscay in December, bound for the River Plate. The atlas already holds Atlantic crossings made in worse boats and on thinner evidence: Brendan's hide-covered curragh, Leif Erikson's landfall at L'Anse aux Meadows in the year 1021. Dumas leaves a paper trail from the first day.
suggested_refs: Port records of Arcachon, December 1931
The 1918 International Eight Metre class sloop Lehg, now at Lujan

stops.name: Rio Grande, aground while asleep
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day unknown, defaulted to January; coordinate corrected from an inland Porto Alegre value to the coastal bar at Rio Grande, the only place the stranding is physically possible
stops.campa: He falls asleep. The Lehg runs onto the bar off Rio Grande do Sul, and the Brazilian Navy comes out and takes him off, and the sloop is refloated and the voyage goes on. Nothing in the record says how long the stranding cost him, or what damage the hull took. Later accounts move the grounding two hundred and fifty kilometres inland to Porto Alegre, at the head of a lagoon no ocean-going sloop can reach while crossing the Atlantic. The pin here is the coastal bar, where a stranding is possible and a navy is at hand.
suggested_refs: Brazilian Navy rescue records for the Rio Grande bar, 1932

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Yacht Club Argentino receives him
stops.date_confidence: attested by the English account and by arithmetic: 13 December 1931 plus the Spanish account's own 121 days lands on 12 April 1932; the rival 12 March 1932, printed one sentence away, is ninety days out and is rejected as an internal corruption
stops.campa: One hundred and twenty-one days out of Arcachon and roughly four thousand five hundred miles alone, he comes up the Plate and berths at the Yacht Club Argentino, on the same stretch of water where Carlos de Alvear stepped off the George Canning in 1812 and where Victoria Ocampo watched an ailing poet disembark in 1924. He is thirty-one and unknown. The sources cannot agree on the day. One says the thirteenth of April, another the twelfth of March, and only the first can be reached by adding his own days to his own departure.
suggested_refs: Yacht Club Argentino arrival book, April 1932
Buenos Aires press coverage of the Lehg's landfall

stops.name: Tigre, Astilleros Parodi builds Lehg II
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January
stops.campa: At the Parodi yard on the Tigre delta, upriver from the port, a ketch is built to his specification: nine metres fifty-five overall, three metres thirty in the beam, an iron keel of three thousand five hundred kilos, and a stern shaped like the bow, so that a following sea meets a point instead of a transom. She is called Lehg II. She is slow. Her shape answers one question, which is what a following sea does to a boat when nobody is on deck to meet it. He has made a single ocean crossing in his life, and he is specifying a hull for the Southern Ocean.
suggested_refs: Astilleros Parodi build records, Tigre, 1934
The surviving hull of Lehg II, Museo Naval de la Nacion

stops.name: The South Atlantic, a full turn on her side
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown, defaulted to January; the position is an open-water approximation on the Rio de Janeiro track, since no fix was recorded, only the turn
stops.campa: On the shakedown run toward Rio de Janeiro the wind reaches a hundred and forty kilometres an hour and rolls Lehg II a full three hundred and sixty degrees about her own keel line. The sails are destroyed. The boat rights herself and he goes on. Afterward he sells her to a Dr. Rafael Gamba, and when the great voyage is finally within reach he has to buy his own boat back from the man he sold her to. The hull he had built for the Southern Ocean spends the years before the war under another man's name.
suggested_refs: The bill of sale of Lehg II to Rafael Gamba, and the later repurchase

segments.name: The Roaring Forties: to the Cape of Good Hope

stops.name: Buenos Aires, ten pounds sterling and no radio
stops.date_confidence: preparation, undated within 1942; placed in the month before sailing
stops.campa: He has ten pounds sterling, lent by a friend, and a year of tinned provisions, because a neutral Argentine sailing into a world at war cannot count on buying food in any belligerent's port. He carries no radio: a small boat transmitting in the South Atlantic would be taken for a spy and sunk by whichever navy heard it first. The helmsmen of the Club Nautico Buchardo help him fit out, with the YMCA of Buenos Aires and the magazine El Grafico. He stuffs newspaper into his clothing against the cold of the forties.
stops.quote: Total para que quiero dinero, si en navegacion no voy a gastar.
stops.quote_source: Vito Dumas, on his lack of funds before the 1942 departure, quoted in es.wikipedia.org, 'Vito Dumas', citing Revista Todo es Historia no. 10, February 1968
suggested_refs: The provisioning list of Lehg II for the 1942 voyage

stops.name: Darsena Norte, Lehg II sails for the three capes
stops.date_confidence: attested; the anchor date from which the voyage's 437-day total is counted
stops.campa: Lehg II leaves the Darsena Norte on a winter morning, bound east and then south, for the Cape of Good Hope, Cape Leeuwin and Cape Horn, every one of them below the fortieth parallel. Fourteen years earlier this same basin received Aime Tschiffely's horses Mancha and Gato, home by sea from New York. He is forty-one, with no radio aboard and no vessel following him, and every ocean on his route is at war. Twenty thousand miles lie ahead of the basin he is leaving.
stops.quote: Voy en esta epoca materialista, a realizar una empresa romantica, para ejemplo de la juventud.
stops.quote_source: Vito Dumas shortly before departure, quoted in es.wikipedia.org, 'Vito Dumas', citing Revista Todo es Historia no. 10, February 1968
suggested_refs: Darsena Norte harbour records, 27 June 1942

stops.name: Montevideo, the last port
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He crosses the Plate and puts into Montevideo, the last land he will see for fifty-five days and the last lit harbour on this side of the ocean. From here the chart holds nothing until Africa. The Uruguayan port is four days from home and already outside the reach of anyone who could help him. After this the only assistance available in the South Atlantic belongs to navies at war, and any of them that finds him will be deciding, with no radio call to guide them, what a lone Argentine ketch is doing down there.
suggested_refs: Montevideo port clearance for Lehg II, July 1942

stops.name: Cape Town, fifty-five days and an infected arm
stops.date_confidence: attested; the mooring is approximated to the Royal Cape Yacht Club in Table Bay
stops.campa: Four thousand five hundred and sixty miles in fifty-five days, and he comes into Table Bay with his right arm so badly infected that he can barely work the ketch. The first of the three capes is behind him. Four hundred years earlier Pedro de Mendoza named a fort on the Parana for Our Lady of Good Hope, in a language that did not yet mean this cape by it. The arm is treated ashore, and Cape Town keeps him three weeks before the leg that will nearly finish him.
suggested_refs: Royal Cape Yacht Club records of the Lehg II's call, August 1942

segments.name: The Indian Ocean and the Terrible Reality

stops.name: Cape Town, out again for New Zealand
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He goes out again on the fourteenth of September for New Zealand: seven thousand four hundred miles across the Indian Ocean and the Southern Ocean, below the fortieth parallel the whole way. There is no port between here and Wellington and no lane that other traffic uses, and south of him the chart holds only ice. He has been three weeks ashore with a bad arm, and the ketch has been in the water since 1934. He provisions and leaves, and by his own account the Atlantic has taught him just enough to measure what is coming.
stops.quote: He pasado en el Atlantico dias terribles: quizas esto me brinda cierta seguridad frente a lo que vendra, pero la realidad de lo que aguarda, la terrible realidad, superara todo lo que haya sufrido en mi vida de marino...
stops.quote_source: Vito Dumas, Los cuarenta bramadores, quoted in es.wikipedia.org, 'Vito Dumas', footnote 9
suggested_refs: Los cuarenta bramadores, the chapters on the Cape Town to Wellington leg

stops.name: Cape Leeuwin, the second cape passed unseen
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source gives a date and none records a sighting; placed mid-leg between 14 September and late December
stops.campa: Somewhere in the southern spring his track crosses the meridian of Cape Leeuwin, far below the Australian coast, and the second of his three capes goes by without being seen. No source gives the day. No source records a sighting. The atlas last came into these latitudes with the United States Exploring Expedition, which sailed in 1838 out of Jeremiah Reynolds's agitation in Congress: six ships and a corps of scientists sent to chart the Antarctic verge. Dumas passes the same verge with one hull, two masts, a compass and a sextant.
suggested_refs: The track chart of Lehg II across the Indian Ocean, reproduced in Los cuarenta bramadores

stops.name: Wellington, landfall after one hundred and four days
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Spanish source gives no arrival date at all, and two independent counts from its own figures converge on 27 and 28 December 1942; the widely repeated 30 November 1942 would make the leg 77 days rather than 104 and the stay 61 days rather than 33
stops.campa: He comes into Port Nicholson one hundred and four days out of Table Bay, seven thousand four hundred miles, and the New Zealanders row out to a boat nobody expected. It is the leg he afterward calls the terrible reality. The date is the weakest point in his whole record: no source gives one, and two separate counts from his own numbers land on the twenty-seventh and the twenty-eighth of December. Half the printed accounts carry a thirtieth of November that his own arithmetic will not support.
suggested_refs: Wellington harbourmaster's record of the arrival of Lehg II, December 1942

stops.name: Wellington, thirty-three days and away
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Thirty-three days in Port Nicholson, refitting a ketch that has been rolled and hammered for three months, and on the thirtieth of January he sails for Valparaiso across the South Pacific. Wellington is the last friendly harbour before Cape Horn. Nobody in it expects to hear whether he arrives, because he has no radio and the next news of him will be news made by his arriving somewhere. He goes out through the heads on an ebb tide and is gone from the record for seventy-two days.
suggested_refs: Port Nicholson clearance papers for Lehg II, 30 January 1943

stops.name: Valparaiso, the Pacific crossed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the French leg table's 72 days added to the attested 30 January departure; no source gives a Valparaiso arrival date, and accounts that place Cape Horn before this landfall have the voyage backwards
stops.campa: Seventy-two days out of New Zealand he raises the Chilean coast and puts into Valparaiso, having crossed the Pacific without major upset. Three ocean legs are behind him. The shortest and worst is ahead. The sources give no date at all for this landfall, and only the arithmetic of the leg supplies one. He is in mid-Pacific in March, not off the Horn, whatever the later summaries say. The great cape belongs to the leg that starts here, from a South American port, heading home.
suggested_refs: Valparaiso port records, April 1943

stops.name: Cape Horn, thrown against the bulkhead
stops.date_confidence: month unknown; the rounding falls inside the 37-day Valparaiso to Mar del Plata leg, which places it roughly between June and August 1943, and not in March as the earlier accounts have it
stops.campa: He rounds it at the first attempt: three thousand two hundred miles from Valparaiso to Mar del Plata in thirty-seven days, and somewhere in the middle of it a blow throws him against a bulkhead and breaks the bone of his nose. His lamp goes out. He writes that he is on the road of death. In 1861 Mikhail Bakunin, escaping Siberia, paid for the Panama Railroad rather than come round this water in a ship with a crew. Dumas comes round it alone, in nine and a half metres, in the southern winter.
stops.quote: Estoy en la ruta de la muerte(...). El viento y el mar son fuertes(...), se apaga mi lampara (...), un fuerte golpe me arroja contra un mamparo(...)
stops.quote_source: Vito Dumas on the Cape Horn passage, quoted in es.wikipedia.org, 'Vito Dumas', citing Cresto in La Nacion, 26 September 2000 (URL now dead); a second fragment in the same paragraph reads 'He pagado barato mi precio por tal osadia (...)'
suggested_refs: Los cuarenta bramadores, the Cape Horn chapter
The Cresto article, La Nacion, 26 September 2000, now unreachable

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a tango called Navegante
stops.date_confidence: the English account gives 5 August 1943 in one place and simply 1943 in another; composer and lyricist are unrecorded in anything reachable
stops.campa: While he is still at sea an Argentine tango is recorded about him. It is called Navegante. The country that will later decide he brings bad luck is at this moment singing about a man it can neither reach nor locate. Nobody has heard anything of Lehg II since Valparaiso, and nobody will until he is sighted off the coast. Neither the composer nor the lyricist is named in any reachable source, and the sources that give the recording a day and the sources that give it only a year do not agree.
suggested_refs: Argentine tango discographies for 1943, entry 'Navegante'

stops.name: Mar del Plata, the first Argentine landfall
stops.date_confidence: reassignment: the Spanish source attaches 8 August 1943 to the Buenos Aires arrival, where it contradicts the 437-day total by thirty days; it fits the Mar del Plata landfall, which the same source names among the ports touched
stops.campa: He touches Argentine ground for the first time in more than a year at Mar del Plata, on the coast of the republic whose far southern territories Julio Argentino Roca organized by law in 1884 and governed from Buenos Aires. The date the sources attach to his arrival at the capital belongs here instead, where it stops contradicting every other figure they print. It is a short coastal run from this port up to the Plate, and for the first time since Montevideo other people can watch him coming.
suggested_refs: Mar del Plata port records, August 1943

stops.name: Buenos Aires, four hundred and thirty-seven days
stops.date_confidence: attested and arithmetically exact: 27 June 1942 plus 437 days is 7 September 1943 to the day, and the Italian account agrees on September; the rival 8 August is thirty days short of the source's own total
stops.campa: He comes up the Plate on a Sunday morning to the harbour he left four hundred and thirty-seven days before. Twenty thousand four hundred and twenty nautical miles. Two hundred and seventy-four of those days actually sailing. Four ports touched. Three capes rounded, every one of them below the fortieth parallel, with one man aboard from the first day to the last. Victoria Ocampo is editing the free French out of this same neutral city while he is gone. The count runs exactly from his own departure date, and the rival date of the eighth of August is thirty days short of his own arithmetic.
stops.quote: la hazana mas inaudita que hombre solo jamas haya cumplido en el mar
stops.quote_source: Jean Merrien, Aux Limites du Possible, on the 1942-43 voyage, in the Spanish rendering given by es.wikipedia.org, 'Vito Dumas'
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires newspapers of 7 and 8 September 1943, the one source that would settle the return date from outside Wikipedia

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Los cuarenta bramadores
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the year of first publication is commonly cited as 1944 and has not been checked against any library catalogue
stops.campa: He writes the voyage himself and calls it Los cuarenta bramadores, the roaring forties, the round of the world by the impossible route. The year of first publication is commonly given as 1944 and has never been checked here against a library catalogue. Adlard Coles publishes an English edition in 1960; an American reissue follows in 2001. The book is the primary evidence for what happened between Cape Town and Wellington, because no other person was present for any of it.
suggested_refs: Los cuarenta bramadores: la vuelta al mundo por la 'ruta imposible'
Alone Through the Roaring Forties, Adlard Coles, 1960
sources: Open Library / Internet Archive edition records

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the second Atlantic circuit begins
stops.date_confidence: year only; no source gives a month for any leg of the 1945 voyage, so every 1945 stop defaults to January and the order is the order of the route
stops.campa: Two years after the circumnavigation he takes Lehg II north on a second Atlantic circuit and calls at Rio de Janeiro in Guanabara Bay, the port he was running toward in 1937 when the boat turned over on him. Seventeen thousand and forty-five miles and two hundred and thirty-four days lie ahead. He will call the account of it El crucero de lo imprevisto, the crossing of the unforeseen, and the sources give no month for any part of it, only a list of ports and a total.
suggested_refs: El crucero de lo imprevisto, Dumas's account of the 1945 voyage

stops.name: Havana, north through the Caribbean
stops.date_confidence: year only; position within the voyage fixed by the route, not by a date
stops.campa: He works north through the Caribbean and puts into Havana. The war in Europe is ending as he sails, and the Atlantic that nearly killed a neutral in 1942 is turning back into a shipping lane. Nothing in the reachable record says how long he stayed, who received him, or what he did with the days ashore. What survives of this whole voyage is a list of ports, a mileage, a day count and a title, and the title is the only part of it that he chose himself.
suggested_refs: Havana harbour records, 1945

stops.name: Coney Island, nearly lost within sight of New York
stops.date_confidence: year only; the Spanish source records the near-disaster without a date and without a precise position within Coney Island waters
stops.campa: Within sight of New York, off the beaches of Coney Island, he nearly dies. The record does not say how, and it gives no date. A man who has crossed the Southern Ocean alone almost loses the boat in the approaches to the busiest harbour on the Atlantic seaboard, within a few miles of the beach. He gets in. This is the same boat that rounded Cape Horn two years earlier and the same man sailing her, and the incident occupies one clause of one sentence in the only account that mentions it. The city that will keep him sick for the better part of a year, ten years from now, receives him for the first time.
suggested_refs: El crucero de lo imprevisto, the New York approach

stops.name: South of the Canaries, the Serantes finds him
stops.date_confidence: year only; no coordinates were recorded for the rescue and this pin is an approximation in open water south of the Canary Islands
stops.campa: On the homeward leg, in open ocean south of the Canary Islands, after one hundred and six days of solitude, the ship Serantes comes up on him and takes him off. No position was written down; this pin is an approximation in empty water. One hundred and six days alone is longer than any single leg of the circumnavigation, and this passage is the one nobody has written about. It is also the only rescue in his record that reaches him in open water rather than at a stranding.
suggested_refs: The log of the ship Serantes, 1945

stops.name: Montevideo, the penultimate port
stops.date_confidence: year only; the Ceara call precedes this one on the same undated homeward run
stops.campa: Ceara first, on the shoulder of Brazil, and then Montevideo again, the same harbour that watched him out for the Southern Ocean in 1942, now the penultimate port of a run of seventeen thousand miles. From here it is one night across the Plate. The Uruguayan capital has seen him leave for the bottom of the world and seen him come back from the North Atlantic, and of the ports outside Argentina it is the one he enters both outbound in 1942 and homeward in 1945.
suggested_refs: Montevideo port records, 1945
Fortaleza, Ceara, the Brazilian call on the homeward leg

stops.name: Buenos Aires, seventeen thousand miles closed
stops.date_confidence: year only; no arrival date is given for the 1945 return
stops.campa: He closes the circuit at Buenos Aires: Rio de Janeiro, Havana, New York, Ceara, Montevideo, seventeen thousand and forty-five miles, two hundred and thirty-four days. He is forty-five. The great voyage is two years behind him, and the country has already made him a figure it argues about rather than a sailor it follows. Lehg II has now carried him round the world by the three capes and up and down the length of the Atlantic, and she will never make another ocean passage under him.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires port records, 1945

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Escuela Nautica Deportiva
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source; the Peron government fell in September 1955, so the honorary commission and the founding of the school necessarily precede that, and the year here is a placement inside the Peronist decade
stops.campa: Peron gives him the honorary rank of Teniente de Navio and the direction of the Escuela Nautica Deportiva, and he founds it and runs it so that people without money can learn to sail. It is the one institution he builds. Later governments attack the idea of it, and the attack sticks to the man. A story spreads that Dumas is mufa, that naming him brings bad luck. The sailor whose voyage the French writer Jean Merrien called the most extraordinary feat a man alone has ever accomplished at sea drifts out of Argentine public memory, except among people who own boats.
suggested_refs: Founding records of the Escuela Nautica Deportiva, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Sirio sails for New York
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: counted back 117 days from the attested 23 September 1955 arrival; the printed departure date of 16 September 1955 falls a week after that arrival and is probably contamination from the coup of that same date, discussed two sentences later in the same article
stops.campa: He sails for New York again, alone, in a smaller boat called Sirio: seven thousand one hundred miles ahead of him and one hundred and seventeen days. He is fifty-four and his health is already going. The departure date usually printed is the sixteenth of September 1955, which is the day of the coup that overthrew his patron and which falls a week after his own arrival in New York. Counting back from that arrival puts him out of the Plate at the end of May, before any of it.
suggested_refs: El viaje del Sirio, Dumas's account of the 1955 passage

stops.name: Hamilton, the calms and the hospital
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the call is attested but undated, and is placed mid-passage between the reconstructed May departure and the attested September arrival; the harbour point is approximated to Hamilton
stops.campa: The equatorial calms hold him and he runs short of water. At Bermuda he is taken to hospital with the signs of scurvy and a blood pressure the record puts at twenty-eight, a number reproduced here exactly as the source gives it because it cannot be read as written. He is fifty-four years old, in a small boat, badly dehydrated, in the middle of a passage he does not abandon. He leaves Hamilton and goes on north toward the coast that Hurricane Ione is about to cross.
suggested_refs: Bermuda hospital admission records, 1955

stops.name: New York, Hurricane Ione and a year of illness
stops.date_confidence: attested, and independently corroborated: Hurricane Ione, which the Spanish source misspells Ionne, came ashore on the American coast on 19 September 1955, four days before
stops.campa: One hundred and seventeen days out, four days after Hurricane Ione comes ashore on the American coast, he brings Sirio into New York. Then he stops. He is ill in the city for close to a year, sells the boat there, and comes home to Argentina as a passenger aboard a freighter, which is the only ocean crossing of his adult life that he does not make himself. In the same twelve months the government that commissioned him is gone, and the men who replaced it have no use for him.
suggested_refs: New York harbour records, September 1955
US Weather Bureau records for Hurricane Ione, 19 September 1955

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Slocum Award for 1956
stops.date_confidence: the award is for the year 1956; no presentation date or place is recorded, and the stop is pinned to his own city rather than to a ceremony nobody described
stops.campa: The Joshua Slocum Society, named for the Nova Scotian who was the first man to sail alone around the world, gives its first Slocum Award for the year 1956, and gives it to Vito Dumas. The citation praises the most notable single-handed passage made during the past year. The society's own page no longer carries that text and the web archive cannot be reached from here, so a footnote in a Spanish encyclopedia is the only surviving carrier of the wording of the first award the society ever made.
stops.quote: the most notable single-handed passage made during the past year
stops.quote_source: Joshua Slocum Society award citation, as reproduced in es.wikipedia.org, 'Vito Dumas', footnote 1, sourced to joshuaslocumsocietyintl.org/awards.htm (page no longer carries the text)
suggested_refs: Joshua Slocum Society International, awards roster

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Sirio II launched
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January
stops.campa: He launches Sirio II at sixty. He is not well, and has not been well since Bermuda. He has made no ocean passage since he sold Sirio in New York five years earlier and came home aboard a freighter as a passenger. No source gives her builder, her rig or her dimensions. Nothing survives of this hull in the reachable record beyond her name, her year, and the fact that she outlasts him in good order: she is restored in 1982 and kept afloat at Mar del Plata by a club whose members never saw him sail her anywhere at all.
suggested_refs: Builder's record for Sirio II, 1961

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Medalla Azul handed over
stops.date_confidence: the presentation is attested to the 1962 skippers' briefing for the Buenos Aires to Rio race; the award year is unresolved, the Cruising Club of America's own roster listing him without a date and secondary accounts giving 1957, while nothing supports the 1943 attribution in circulation
stops.campa: At the briefing where the skippers of the Buenos Aires to Rio race are given their final instructions, the Blue Water Medal of the Cruising Club of America is put into his hands. The club's own roster lists him without a date. Secondary accounts give 1957. Nothing at all supports attaching it to the circumnavigation that plainly earned it. He is sixty-one, receiving in a race briefing an American medal for a voyage made nineteen years earlier, in a country that has half decided he is unlucky.
suggested_refs: Cruising Club of America Blue Water Medal roster

stops.name: Cabo Polonio, the race abandoned
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January, and it is the same race whose briefing produced the medal
stops.campa: He starts the race and gives it up off Cabo Polonio, where the Uruguayan coast turns and the lighthouse stands on its rock among the sea lions. He is ill. The boat is sound, and the crewed fleet goes on to Rio without him. It is the only recorded occasion in his life on which Vito Dumas turns back from a passage he has begun, and the sea has nothing to do with it. He is one day out of the Plate, in company, on coastal water he had crossed before without incident.
suggested_refs: Results of the 1962 Buenos Aires to Rio de Janeiro ocean race

stops.name: Mar del Plata, the last passage
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January
stops.campa: His last voyage is a coastal run from Buenos Aires down to Mar del Plata, a passage a weekend sailor makes, over water he first crossed coming home from Cape Horn. He is sixty-three and has one year to live. Nothing in the reachable record says who was aboard with him, how long it took, or whether he understood it as the last one. The port he ends at is the port where he first touched Argentine soil in 1943, coming up from Cape Horn after four hundred days of ocean.

stops.name: Vicente Lopez, the stroke
stops.date_confidence: attested; the precise site within Vicente Lopez is not specified
stops.campa: He dies of a cerebrovascular accident at Vicente Lopez, on the northern edge of Buenos Aires, at sixty-four. He had sailed alone around the world by the three great capes in the middle of a world war, without a radio, in a boat nine and a half metres long, and had come home to a country that would spend the next thirty-five years deciding what to do about it. The Argentine Navy, in which he holds an honorary rank given by a president now in exile, will decide eventually.

stops.name: Cementerio de Olivos, the first grave
stops.date_confidence: the burial date is not recorded anywhere reachable and falls within days of the death; the plot is approximated to the cemetery grounds
stops.campa: He is buried at the Cementerio de Olivos, a few kilometres from the house where he died and a short way inland from the river he learned to sail on. The burial date is not written down in anything reachable. He lies here for thirty-five years, through the governments that disliked his politics and through the story that he was bad luck, in a suburban cemetery with no naval connection and no water in sight of it. Nothing reachable records who attended, or what was said.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Konex diploma
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month is given for the award
stops.campa: Fifteen years dead, he is given the Konex Diploma al Merito in yachting, on the Argentine institution's roll of the country's greatest sportsmen. It is the first sign of the rehabilitation: the man the mufa story pushed out of public memory is put back on a list, in a category, among athletes, by a jury with no interest in who once commissioned him or which government fell afterward. The decade that follows will put his boats into museums and his head into bronze on a seafront.

stops.name: Club Nautico Mar del Plata, Sirio II afloat
stops.date_confidence: restoration year attested; month unknown, and the club mooring is approximated
stops.campa: Sirio II is restored and moored at the Club Nautico of Mar del Plata, kept in good order by a club that treats her as an heirloom. She is the last boat he owned and the least famous of them, launched by a sick man of sixty who never took her anywhere the world noticed and gave up her only race off Cabo Polonio. The restoration is dated to 1982; no month is given for it, and the source names nobody who carried it out. She floats. Of his three principal vessels she is the only one still on the water rather than standing under a roof with her keel dry.

stops.name: Mar del Plata, the bust on the Boulevard Maritimo
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the day is not given, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: A bust by Hidelberg Ferrino is set at the corner of the Boulevard Maritimo and Carlos Pellegrini, facing the sea he came in from in 1943 on the last leg out of Cape Horn. Mar del Plata claims him: the port of his final passage, the harbour where his last boat lies afloat, and now the corner where his head stands in bronze above the traffic on the seafront. It is twenty-one years after his death, six years after the Konex jury put him back on a list, and fourteen years before the Navy comes for his bones.

stops.name: Chacarita, moved to the Panteon Naval
stops.date_confidence: the source dates the transfer to 2000 or later; month and day unknown, defaulted to January, and the plot is approximated to the cemetery grounds
stops.campa: His remains are lifted out of Olivos and carried to the Panteon Naval in the Cementerio de la Chacarita, among the naval dead of the republic. It takes thirty-five years. The move closes the argument the mufa story kept open: whatever Argentina thought of his politics, the country files him at the end with its sailors, in a pantheon he entered by an honorary commission from a fallen president and by one voyage that no navy on earth could have ordered a man to make.

stops.name: Lujan, the Lehg in the museum
stops.date_confidence: undated in every reachable source; the year on this stop is a placeholder and carries no evidentiary weight
stops.campa: The Lehg, the eight-metre sloop he took out of Arcachon in 1931 knowing nothing about the open sea, stands in the museum complex at Lujan with his compass, his sextant, a boom iron, and a map of her crossing. She is inland now, sixty kilometres from tidewater, on the pampa, among carriages and locomotives and the stuffed horses of other men's journeys. The instruments in the case with her are the ones he steered by while he slept through the Brazilian coast. No source records when she arrived there, who gave her, or what condition she was in when she came.

stops.name: Tigre, Lehg II under a roof
stops.date_confidence: undated in every reachable source for both the donation and the restoration; the year on this stop is a placeholder, and the only fixed date in the boat's afterlife is the 1966 wreck at the mouth of the port of La Plata
stops.campa: Lehg II is given to the Argentine Navy for training, wrecked at the mouth of the port of La Plata in 1966, salvaged, left to deteriorate, restored at last and put under a roof at the Museo Naval de la Nacion in Tigre, a few kilometres from the Parodi shed where she was built in 1934. Twenty thousand four hundred and twenty miles and three capes, then a training hull, then a wreck, then a display. Neither the donation nor the restoration is dated in anything reachable.
